summary:
South Korea does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available and the requirement of surgery is falling. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that forcing surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. The Supreme Court has also allowed a transgender person with minor children to change their gender in the family relations register.

Trans visitors have a documented, judicially enforced right to public restrooms. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court issued a final, unappealed ruling that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, awarding 300,000 won in symbolic compensation against the state.

There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on these grounds. In healthcare, the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner. The Constitutional Court did issue a landmark 2024 ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights, extending a measure of recognition in that specific area.

For a visitor on the ground, Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are broadly positive, but the surrounding context requires care: organised conservative opposition is active, no national anti-discrimination law exists, and Human Rights Watch records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in its 2025 world report, which also notes a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.
tangentialFactors:
Research by the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, found that transgender teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding in urine and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments. This is a resident-facing pattern rather than a visitor rule, but it indicates the depth of outing anxiety the visitor may encounter in practice.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published in Epidemiology and Health on 27 June 2025 followed 585 transgender and non-binary young adults across life stages, documenting a pervasive discrimination burden at school, in the workplace and in transition-related care.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 also covers the December 2024 martial-law crisis and assembly freedoms, part of a turbulent domestic political environment that shapes public order conditions for visitors.

South Korea sits in a period of rapid social change alongside entrenched institutional resistance, which is why rights that exist in court judgments are unevenly realised in administration.
localsOnly:
Registration rights for LGBT organisations have been contested through the courts rather than simply granted: an NGO won at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed to the Seoul High Court and the Supreme Court, while Human Rights Watch criticised years of bureaucratic obstruction of LGBT group registration. LGBTI organisations can now register.

The Supreme Court permits a transgender person with minor children to change their gender in the family relations register, removing a family-law barrier that in many jurisdictions blocks recognition entirely.

Transgender people are excluded from South Korean military service, and Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su's case shows how the armed forces treat transition. A transgender conscript, she was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Nationwide survey data shows discrimination accumulating across school, work and transition-related care for trans and non-binary young adults.
outOfScopeNotes:
The consequence axis of an arrest remains unresolved on the civilian side: no source in this inventory describes how transgender prisoners are housed in South Korea's civilian prison system. There is no birth-sex versus identity placement rule, no special unit, and no solitary or segregation practice recorded, and no civilian trans-prisoner case surfaced.

The Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor entry on the Supreme Court's decision permitting a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register returned HTTP 403 and could not be retrieved at research time; the claim rests on the entry's title and metadata rather than the full text.

No source here reports a hate-crime statute or aggravated-penalty provision covering offences motivated by gender identity or sexual orientation, and none confirms whether police or prosecutors apply any such charging enhancement in practice. This is not sourced either way.

Whether a foreign visitor can present identity documents whose marker matches their presentation at Korean immigration is not addressed by any source in this inventory.
